speechtext: I may say that this was a technical error and we took it up with the chief electoral officer. I also spoke to the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) who went into the matter carefully and the amendment was drafted in conference with the chief electoral officer. I move the amendment accordingly.
Possibly the hon. member for East Calgary will explain the effect of the amendment.

There is no alteration
whatever in the agreed boundaries. The northern boundary of a very small portion was omitted from the original description as it is in the schedule. When I was speaking to the chief electoral officer, he said that he thought it would be preferable to have the amendment as suggested. He stated that he had the power to make the change when he came to officiate, but he would prefer to have it put into this new schedule.

Amendment agreed to.
Schedule as amended agreed to.
Schedule-Yukon Territory-agreed to on division.
On the schedule-Quebec.

As there were several technical errors in the bill as originally printed and some changes have occurred since, I move, seconded by Mr. Tetreault, that the schedule of the bill with respect to the province of Quebec be stricken out and the following substituted therefor. The substitution is in the terms of the schedule as it appears in the reprinted bill.

So far as this schedule is concerned, there has been no change from the original schedule as regards the twenty-five constituencies which are considered as being in the district of Quebec. Twenty-

three put of those twenty-five are being altered in some way or another. I do not desire ito repeat my objections to those changes. I expressed my views three days ago and they stand as I expressed them on that occasion. Since then I have received many letters of protest from various constituencies, one letter in particular from Causapscal which was transferred to Bonaventure, being couched in language which would hardly conform to parliamentary rules. I desire again merely to register my protest as to all those changes, more particularly with regard to Temiscouata, Levis, L'Islet-Montmagny and Dorchester. I will ask the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), who is at present in the chamber, to give the committee the reasons for the change contained in the schedule with respect to his constituency. The municipalities of St. Luc, St. Maxime, St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie are being transferred, St. Luc being placed in the constituency of Bellechasse and the three others in the constituency of Beauce. I will ask my hon. friend to give us the particular reasons for which each one of these changes is made.
I would suggest that the hon. member proceed with his speech and afterwards I shall be entitled to answer.
I think I am entitled to know the reasons for these changes. Why does my hon. friend favour the throwing of those four municipalities into other constituencies?
I was not a member of the redistribution committee, but I am not afraid to speak.

I would ask a member
of the committee, a member of the government or, indeed, anybody to give the reasons we should approve these changes in the county of Dorchester.

I shall speak right now
if the hon. gentleman insists, because he might say in another quarter that I am afraid to answer him.
The hon. member is afraid to keep those parishes.

Will the hon. member
keep calm and quiet. I cannot answer three or four hon. gentlemen at once. The reasons for these changes are very clear. First of all,
I may say, at the outset of my remarks, that in spite of the fact that the so-called conciliation committee was formed last week in order to reach some agreements, I think I can safely

Redistribution Bill
state with respect to Quebec that the hon. member for Quebec East has not at any time been willing to come to any arrangement; what he did was only to repudiate the arrangements which had been made with the hon. gentleman of the Liberal party who was on the redistribution committee. I think when an hon. gentleman wishes to make some change in his constituency, the first thing he ought to do is to try to see the hon. member representing the neighbouring county where the different parishes will have to be joined. What he has to do is to see that the members of his party who are on the redistribution committee, make an arrangement with the member who represents the other party. The arrangement was made between the Conservative members of the committee and the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) that, with respect to Dorchester, the parish of St. Luc would be joined to Bellechasse and the parishes of St. Maxime, St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie would be joined to Beauce'. So far as Beauce is concerned, the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Lacroix) agreed to accept those parishes. He agreed to such an extent that the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) stated the other day in this house in the presence of the hon. member for Quebec East that the hon. member for Beauce had put in writing that he agreed to accept the parishes of St. Maxime, St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie. This has not been denied. The parish of St. Maxime in Dorchester it is true has belonged to the electoral division of Dorchester for provincial purposes for about twenty years. But up to the year 1924 the citizens of St. Maxime always voted in 'the electoral division of Beauce.
I have here a statement of all the electoral returns from the year 1900 up to the year 1930. I shall not take up the time of the committee to give the figures, but I can do so if I am challenged by the hon. member for Quebec East. It appears from the electoral returns that the citizens of St. Maxime have voted in the electoral division of Beauce up until the year 1925, but in the Redistribution Act of 1924, upon the demand of the former Solicitor General, the parish of St. Maxime was joined to the electoral division of Dorchester.
With respect to the parishes of St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie, in the Redistribution Act of 1924 they were described as being in the township of Metgermette and Metgermette North. Those parishes always up to 1931 belonged to the provincial county of Beauce. It is true that for twenty-five years the citizens of those parishes had voted in the district of Dorchester for electoral purposes, but nevertheless the parishes of Metgermette, Metgermette North, St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie had up to 1931 always belonged to the electoral division of Beauce for provincial purposes.
But after I had been elected member for Dorchester in 1930 the provincial government, following its usual tactics of changing electoral divisions at its will and fancy, began to make changes in a great number of counties which had elected Conservative members for federal purposes. I have here the statutes of Quebec,
21	George Y, 1930-31, and I would refer the hon. member for Quebec East to chapter 15, section 1 of which reads as follows:
The township of Metgermette North and that portion of the municipality of the north part of the township of Metgermette North forming part of the electoral district of Beauce are detached from such electoral district and annexed, for electoral purposes to the electoral district of Dorchester.
The hon. gentleman challenged the member for Stanstead the other day to quote one instance of a provincial change in provincial electoral divisions. There is one change.
I would also refer the hon. gentleman to the same statutes, 21 George V, 1930-31, chapter 16, section 1 of which reads as follows:
The lots of the tenth, eleventh and twelfth ranges of the official plan and book of reference of the cadastre for the township of Ware are detached from the electoral district of Bellechasse and annexed to the electoral district of Dorchester, for all purposes including school purposes, and as to such school purposes, from the next school year, and are declared to have formed part in the past, for school purposes, of the parish municipality of Ste. Sabine, county of Bellechasse; they are declared to form part of the parish municipality of St. Luc, county of Dorchester.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in 1931-32 not only did the provincial government annex the provincial parishes of St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie to the county of Dorchester for electoral purposes, but they also attached some lots from Ste. Sabine in the county of Bellechasse to the county of Dorchester.
In a statute passed in the following year,
22	George V, 1931-32, chapter 18, section 6 provides as follows:
The name of the township municipality of Metgermette North is changed, by this act, into that of the "municipality of St. Zacharie," and the name of the municipality of the north part of the township of Metgermette North is changed, by this act, into that of the "municipality of Ste. Aurelie."
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, when the first bill was drafted the members of the committee, including the Liberal members, were
Redistribution Bill

not aware apparently of the changes which had been made by the provincial government since the Redistribution Act of 1924, and consequently when they drafted the bill they did not insert the names of Metgermette North, St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie. But when the so-called conciliatory committee sat last week, the hon. member for Quebec East did not object to the changing of St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie because he stated himself to the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) and the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion) that he had no objection to the removal of the parishes of St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie from the electoral division of Dorchester to the adjoining electoral division of Beauce. But now that the bill comes before the house and amendments have been made only in order to meet the difficulty which has arisen in view of the change made in the boundaries of the county of Dorchester by the legislature of Quebec in 1931 and 1932, the hon. gentleman from Quebec East, only with a view to making political capital, tries to make this committee believe that some new changes have been made since the printing of this bill. Such an opinion is absolutely unworthy of the high reputation of the hon. gentleman who, as I repeat, stated last week that he had nc objection to the parishes of Ste. Aurelie and St. Zacharie, which had always belonged for provincial purposes to the county of Dorchester, being joined to the county of Beauce. As I stated in my speech the other day the hon. gentleman last week in his speech said that people resented being changed from one district to another for voting purposes. Well, Mr. Chairman, if people resent having to vote in another district, I think the electors of the county of Dorchester will resent the fact that their majority might be swollen or drowned by the votes of the people living in the division of Beauce T think, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that I am perfectly in order in asking that the limits of Dorchester comprise the electors of the county of Dorchester alone. I think those details are sufficient, but if the hon. gentleman has something else to say I shall ask permission to answer him later.
I shall ignore the personal attacks of my hon. friend.

There were no personal
attacks.
He has demonstrated the truth of the maxim that when one has no case the best thing to do is to abuse the other party.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Abuse the attorney.

However, I shall try,
Mr. Chairman, even from my hon. friend's own statement to demonstrate how unfair this Change is in Dorchester county.
First, the parish of St. Luc, which gives a strong Liberal majority, has never been elsewhere than in the county of Dorchester.
It is a place which when it was erected as a municipality was situated in the county of . Dorchester, and it was erected civilly and canonically, as we say in the province of Quebec, in the constituency of Dorchester, and placed there for all purposes, and it is now being put in Bellechasse because it gives a strong Liberal majority.
As to the other place, namely St. Maxime de Scott, it was erected in 1895, canonically and civilly, in 1897 and was placed in the county of Dorchester. It always was part of the county of Dorchester, provinoially, and was not added to that county federally be- . cause, if hon. members will look at the redistribution acts of 1924, 1903 and previously they will find that so far as the schedule in the province of Quebec was concerned it was stated that the counties of the province of Quebec would remain as at that time constituted except in certain particulars. So, when there was no mention of any change the counties remained as they were federally, and the provincial changes did not affect the constitution of the federal ridings. St. Maxime de Scott voted provinoially in Dorchester all the time, and as there was no mention of it in the federal redistribution act it continued to vote in the county of Beauce until in 1924, at which time the provincial counties were accepted as the basis, except where changes had been made.	_
It has been stated that those changes have been made there and automatically applied to the federal redistribution act because the province of Quebec had a Liberal government. Let me tell the committee that when in 1897 St. Maxime de Scott was declared by the legislature of Quebec to be in the county of Dorchester, that province was under a Conservative government headed by the late Mr. Flynn, and the provincial member for Dorchester, the Hon. L. P. Pelletier, Conservative, was attorney general. On January 9. 1897 the legislature of Quebec erected the parish of St. Maxime de Scott, at that time stating it was part of the county of Dorchester.
As I have stated, had the changes been made in 1924 we would have had no objection to the undoing-to use the Prime Minister's word-of what had been done. According to all principles, St. Maxime de Scott is and

Redistribution-Mr. Ferland
should be in Dorchester. But because automatically in 1924, after being in Beauce federally it was transferred to Dorchester, I had no real objection to its being replaced in Beauce, because I have stated that I had no objection to the Prime Minister undoing what he said had been done in 1924. But if that argument applies to St. Maxime de Scott, why not to Ste. Aurelie and St. Zacharie? I have consulted all the electoral reports and although St. Zacharie and Ste. Aurelie were in Beauce provincially, they were in the federal district of Dorchester not only in 1924, 1914 and in 1903, but before that. I went even to the election of 1887, when Mr. Duchesnay and Mr. Lesage were candidates in Dorchester. Those places have always been part of the county of Dorchester. Surely my hon. friend does not want to throw them away because in 1924 they were placed in his constituency. They were there before that. When the other day I said I would have no objection, because I had been told that federally they had been in Beauce, I was misinformed, because I find that they were not. I have learned that they were and have always been part of the county of Dorchester. So my hon. friend is taking four Liberal strongholds and sending one to Bellechasse and three others to Beauce. I say it is unfair for him to try to select his own constituency in that way. I say that the people in that constituency who elected him in 1930 will resent his action and I protest against the change. It is manifestly unfair, and cannot be justified or excused. It has been done for political purposes, and my denunciation of such practices will not be confined to this place.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to deliver a long spech. I simply wish to add a few personal observations to the vehement protests of the opposition against this proposal to redistribute the federal electoral districts, which, as we have noted, is not colourless, scentless or tasteless. In a word, I consider this bill reeks with the most odious stupidity and fanaticism that was ever found in any piece of legislation unless one excepts possibly what was labelled the " Stolen Wartime Elections' Act."
The bill converts the electoral boundaries of the province of Quebec into a regular jigsaw puzzle. I know the words which I might utter and the remarks I might make will bring about no change, since the Government with its haughty and arrogant majority may accomplish anything and has the power to enact this legislation.
The Conservative party submitted three projects respecting the county of Joliette during the consideration of this bill. By the first project inscribed on the electoral map which we found at the sub-committee on redistribution, they had first of all annexed the county of Montcalm to Joliette minus St. Donat where the electors give a majority to the Liberal party. They had also thought of adding the parish of Lavaltrie to Joliette and to take away at the same time from Joliette the parishes of St. Paul and Crabtree-Mills. They were annexed to L'Assomption whose population totals 15,323; then, they took that part of L'Assomption and united it to the Island of Montreal, with a population of 50,000. In the face of our protests, our friends of the Conservative party were not slow in realizing that this was a stupid project and told us not to waste any time in discussing it as they were going to abandon it.
Then, they submitted a second project to us. Before being modified, it involved the transfer of the entire county of Montcalm to the county of Joliette. I have had occasion of visiting my county since the debate on this bill got under way, and the people of my county told me they approved this project- at least those whom I met at Joliette where they go to transact business. They stated they were quite satisfied with the proposed union of the county of Montcalm with Joliette. It was quite logical, for the county of Montcalm forms part of our judicial district, it forms part of the diocese of Joliette and the citizens of Montcalm go regularly to Joliette on business matters. So the people seem to be delighted to have their county annexed to the county of Joliette.
Since then, in view of the injustice done to the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm, a new readjustment was proposed and the latter county will form with Joliette the finest diocese in the province of Quebec and will henceforth be called the county of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. From a religious standpoint, all the electors of the county of Montcalm, as I have said, also a few parishes of the county of L'Assomption form part of the diocese of Joliette. The new county as proposed in the bill becomes certainly the largest, perhaps the most populous, and the most beautiful county in the province of Quebec. It comprises two classical colleges, one at L'Assomption and the other at Joliette; three very distinguished provincial members in the person of my friends, Messrs. Reid, Duval and Bastien, respectively members for L'Assomption, Montcalm and Berthier; a Legislative Councillor, my very distinguished friend Notary Daniel; a senator no less distinguished, the Hon. Mr. Casgrain, finally, a town of the importance of Joliette. This new
Redistribution-Mr. Ferland

county will have a population of 56,773. I may add that you will also find among the provincial members, my excellent friend, Mr. Lucien Dugar, of Joliette.
The population of this county is divided as follows: Joliete, 27,585; L'Assomption, 15,323; Montcalm, 13,987. The two counties of Joliette and L'Assomption-Montcalm had the following population: the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm, 29,188 and Joliette, 27,585. You can see that the two counties contained a sufficiently large population without the necessity of adding thereto. They would have been justified in increasing the population of Argenteuil which is less than 30,000. It is a crying injustice to increase the county of Joliette to such a great extent by annexing thereto L'Assomption-Montcalm to give it a rural population of more than 40,000 and an urban population in excess of 15,000, when the population of neighbouring counties is much smaller.
Take Three Rivers, for instance. The member for this constituency who took good care of his seigniory simply gave himself electors in his city to the number of about forty thousand. It is said he is afraid of the " country " and he rid himself of the rural parts of his county.

Of the
Liberal sections only.

\Ye find in Berthier-Maskinonge a population of only 30,000. The hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Baribeau) that dauntless fellow who fears the coming elections, took good care to delimit his county in such a manner as to retain a population of only about twenty thousand. They created a new county in the region, St. Maurice-Lafleche, which also has a population of only about thirty thousand souls. As for Joliette and Montcalm which constitute a magnificent region, which form beautiful counties, they said: We -will make them larger, more beautiful and they will find men sufficiently industrious and qualified to represent a lot of people. The likes and consent of the electors count for little, we will create a county with a population of 57,000 souls in a region that covers an area of more than one hundred miles, this no matter whether it suits or does not suit the people of these counties.
The salient feature of the present redistribution bill, Mr. Chairman, is the fact that the Conservative party went to great pains to create for itself nice little sky-blue counties and to achieve this end, to form large Liberal strongholds, solidly Liberal. The redistri-

bution project is not fair to the Conservatives of the county of Joliette. In that county the Conservatives had an even chance of electing one of their representatives from time to time, as they did succeed in the past. With Joliette-Montcalm, there still remained some prospect of electing, perhaps one of these days, a Conservative candidate, and I know that one of the most eminent Conservatives of my district-who became a judge -I will not say in what court, expressed the opinion one day that the Conservatives would win the county of Joliette the day it was united to Montcalm. But it is evident now that the Liberal stronghold of L'Assomption-Montcalm is annexed to Joliette, that my friends of Joliette for whom I have much sympathy, have lost all their chances. They will tell the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Sauve) who had his party in opposition at Quebec financed by one of my friends, Mr. Jos. Dufresne, a former provincial member, they will say: Sir, you are satisfied with your work, now that you have immolated us on the political altar in order to secure for yourselves small Conservative counties in the province of Quebec!
May I put a question to the hon. member?
Certainly.

The hon. member has just stated that the new county of Champlain will have a population of about 20,000 souls. I will tell him that the population will total 37,500, about double the figure he has just mentioned.
You rid yourself of 15,000.
I knew my hon. friend had taken care to decrease the population of his county considerably. I quoted these figures from memory, but the principle remains the same.
There is a very great difference.

My hon.
friend lacked courage. He was elected by a population of about 45,000 or 50,000 and he became frightened on the eve of the election and said to himself: I cannot be reelected member at Ottawa if I retain that population, because I did not carry out any of the promises which my leader and I made to my people.

We will see as to that later on.

Redistribution-Mr. Ferland
It is extraordinary to see how badly our friends look after their interests in the province of Quebec.

They are
real cowards.

People are crying out in all parts of the province of Quebec that the project is unjust and hurts the Conservative party. They are so afraid of the people that they listen to the protests that come from all sides, from Conservatives as well as Liberals, ad they persist in wanting to have this bill approved. The most beautiful photograph of their stupid project was presented in one of our newspapers, L'Action Populaire, of Joliette, which in a remarkable article dated April 30, 1933, and written by my good friend, the Rev. Albini Lafortune, priest, gives the following sketch: The party in power, he states, usually avails itself of the opportunity to enlarge its fief or consolidate its positions. In the circumstances, there is no better tailor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
The hon. member knows it is strictly forbidden by the rule to read newspaper articles commenting a debate or a question actually under discussion in the house.
Talking about the tailor, as the Evenement says, when one carves out a county, one may also ride to a fall.

To sum up, this article states-I can at least comment on it-he runs the scissors as he likes through the home-spun cloth; he cuts to the right, cuts to the left, scallops on the sides; he lengthens one end, shortens at the other end; destroys here, patches there.

It is a
counterpane 1

(Translation):	To put
it in a nutshell, he tries to dye as much as possible according to his own colour. I think, sir, you are well advised to prevent me from reading what the newspapers say about this infamous bill. It is very clever of you, sir, to suggest to me not to read what the newspapers have written in that connection.
I am not preventing the hon. member, the rule prevents him.

The session
would last until New Year's Day.

Even the
Conservative newspapers insulted you. Who could ever have thought that the Conservatives of my province whom I love, esteem and admire and for all of whom I bespeak fair treatment, would find themselves in this situation? Did you ever conceive a more shocking spectacle than that of this great Conservative party being insulted even in Conservative newspapers? You all know what the Evene-mernt said about you, Conservatives of Quebec, in its issue of May 22 relevant to this iniquitous measure we are now considering. Everybody knows that the Evenement is a great Conservative daily, loyal to the Government party, loyal to the Ottawa Conservatives. In its issue of May 22, that newspaper went so far as to state that the Quebec Conservatives who advise the right honourable Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) are fools. They even used a language that is unparliamentary; they used a language I would be compelled to withdraw were I to use it in the House of Commons.
The hon. member does not use it, but he is on the border line.
There remains very little after that!
They stated among other things that the Prime Minister's French-Canadian advisers are good fellows, if you will, but not very intelligent
They are not advice-boats!	.

Fortunately
they are good fellows.

But they
are not brave fellows.

Protest
against the insults of the Evenement, do not let them say such harsh things about you! Defend yourselves against such attacks! If you are not courageous enough when it comes to appear before those who elected you, be at least courageous in defending the rights of your race.

Order!
The hon. member must not address his colleagues. If he has harsh comments to make, let him address them to me-

The Soleil
said less than the Evenement.

(Translation): Mr. Chairman, I was addressing myself to my country over your head. My learned colleagues to the right believed perhaps that I was addressing



Redistribution-Mr. Ferland
myself to them. I will address them shortly in another language; I will be courteous and polite.

One sure
thing, the hon. member did not address himself to his pair in that manner.

We do not
belong to the same family!

One must
not forget that he is not my father in the natural order of things, otherwise I would have a poor father. He is a charming fellow, naturally, who honours me greatly by pairing with me. Our friends generally-I will name nobody, since I must address myself to you, Mr. Chairman-our friends wanted through the remaking of the electoral map to carve out little counties which they believed "sure things," which they believed unmistakably Conservative. They wanted to carve out counties which I might call, permanent, ever lasting. One would imagine that taking their inspiration from our ancestral traditions they wanted to imitate our Canadians of old, who, in marriage contracts, always gave their daughter " an everlasting cow and a reasonable pig." I can see your efforts to be delivered of an everlasting cow, but I do not find your pig reasonable.
Hear! hearl

Mr. Chairman, the worst feature about this bill is not the fact my county has -been enlarged, that they have created a diocese for me, it is not the fact some of my friends will have much more work and many more people-we do not fear the people, the more we have the happier we are-but the fact that even Conservative newspapers like the Montreal Gazette, independent newspapers, like Le Devoir, l'Action Populaire, l'Evenement, have found that we French-Canadians must everlastingly be the dupes-that is what I do not like.
Mr. Chairman-, fear is evidently what characterizes our hon. friends to the right. It is said fear is the beginning of wisdom, and they deem wise to seize the opportunity to rid themselves of many counties, of a large number of people who elected them. They are all afraid. They removed from each of the counties which they reduced in size a certain number of electors because they considered them Liberals.

They are
afflicted with colic.

I am sure it is because they are afraid. Thus, the hon. member for Champlain who interrupted me a

moment ago might be justified in being afraid. For all that, he is a good fellow.
He is not very brave.

He has not had as great an opportunity to distribute political favours as our minister. As for our French-Canadian ministers is it not astonishing to see how afraid they are, how they are frightened, notwithstanding the fact they gave positions, replaced postmasters, expended possibly hundreds of thousands of dollars holding investigations and making changes in post offices, and have important " patronage " at their disposal. How does it happen they are afraid?
A minister in a small county such as Cham-bly-Vercheres whose population is not very large would be afraid of his electors? A minister, a barrister in Montreal who did us honour as batonnier, who has a big voice, who speaks loud, who makes many promises at election time and who even erected a monument to himself by building with unemployment relief money on the banks of the St. Lawrence a wall that resembles those monuments one finds on the Marne or at Verdun and which are nothing else than monuments erected to the memory of the dead! Since when does one erect monuments during one's lifetime? Has he a presentiment that he is going to die when he erects such a monument to himself on the shores of the St. Lawrence? When we pass that spot on our way to Montreal, we see this monument, this large cement wall in front of which the beautiful St. Lawrence river traversing the region of Montreal flows by.

He is so to
speak an unreliable minister.

There is no doubt about it; my -hon. friend is right when he says he is an unreliable minister. He trembles so much he cannot conceal his fear. It is true he is the leader of the marine boys, but he does not wear tlhe sailor's wide-legged trousers to hide his shivering limbs when the electors approach.
They should give him a " tam-o'-shanter " to wear.

Is it not
astonishing, Mr. Chairman, to see the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) tremble. Has he reason to fear?

He is accustomed to run away.

Redistribution-Mr. Ferland

The hon.
Postmaster General has a small county, Laval-Two-Mountains. This county was sympathetic to him to the extent of electing his son to the Quebec legislature.

He wanted
to have it wizened up.

It is astonishing to see that the hon. Postmaster General is also afraid of his electors. The municipalities of Pont-Viau and Laval-des-Rapides are in the Laval-Two Mountains district. It is said French-Canadians live in that district. Is he afraid of the rapids? He fears that in retaining Laval-des-Rapides he will be carried away by the rising wave of the people and he transfers them to my friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Jean). It is amusing to note that our Franch-Canadian representatives who have power, " patronage " and might should be such cowards. Yet, one would have expected from the hon. Postmaster General a vehement protest against anything that savoured of injustice. I remember, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. Postmaster General always had countless virtues in the province of Quebec.

He never
practised them.

He was for a long time leader of the Opposition and he was so virtuous that the prime minister, Mr. Taschereau, and his party wanted to keep him always at Quebec. Had the Quebec people not discovered New Zealand butter in 1930, thev probably would not have lost their opposition leader. I have heard him sometimes in the course of patriotic addresses, moralizing on everything and nothing. He asks us to follow the ancestral traditions, and to practise the virtue of justice. It is extraordinary that people like him allow such injustices to be committed. I would like to give you an example showing how Mr. Sauve -I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman; I withdraw; I should not have named him, I broke the rule unintentionally, I am very sorry. Here is what the hon. Postmaster General said in 1921. He was better than us, he was better than you, Mr. Chairman, because he said things. ... A friend tells me the comparison is odious. I have much sympathy for you, Mr. Chairman, you are one of my colleagues at the Bar, I must be very careful as you might be appointed judge some day and I would not want to jeopardize the interests of my people in the cases which you might hear. I would rather offer you compliments.

The electorate evidently displayed the resentment they harboured for a long time against the federal government. . . Since 1911, the Ottawa government has been a source of care and trials for the old party of Cartier in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman,
I wish to raise a point of order. I have listened with impatience and patience-with both feelings

to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Ferland). I claim he has no right to speak as he has done for the past ten minutes and I believe I am perfectly right in calling the hon. member to order. On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, it is not a question of discussing the merit of the counties of L'Assomption, Joliette and Montcalm. It is the

He failed In

Order,
gentlemen!

Will the

On the

I am therefore compelled to give the member for Joliette the same latitude as is given others and to declare the point raised is not well taken.

What 1
was going to say, when the hon. minister did me the honour of interrupting me, was that

he found his party had been more Tory than Conservative, from 1911 to 1921. At that time, it was no virtue to be a Tory, it was a dreadful crime. My hon friend said his letter published in La Presse on December 7, 1921, was corrected later on-

I never sent
any such letter to La Presse I repeat La Presse made a correction on December 9 and stated there had been a mistake.
The hon. member is bound to accept the hon. minister's denial.

I accept
his denial. I merely want to ask him whether La Presse published a letter bearing his signature in its issue of December 7, 1921?
Yes, but there was a mistake, as I have just shown.
The letter was published by mistake? That is to say it was not intended for the newspapers?
I do not have to undergo a cross-examination at the hands of the hon. member.

I will not

Precisely, that

I wish to
be courteous, gracious, and not avail myself of every opportunity to trample on my opponents.

It is easy
when they are on all fours.
I now refer to the fear of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion), my pair. He was in his seat a moment ago. I see him conversing with the right hon. Prime Minister.
It is not the member for Quebec-Montmorency, it is the member for Quebec West (Mr. Dupre).

West and
South.

My hon.
friend from Quebec West is also in a blue funk on the eve of the election.

An hon. MEMBER (Translation): That is natural.

He had
another kind of fear, fear of Quebec's solid Liberal "bloc" and of Liberal domination in the province of Quebec. As he candidly admitted to us the other day, with redistribution as effected: "We are sure now that there will no longer be any solid Liberal "bloc." Liberal domination in the province of Quebec is ended," he said. If he means he is afraid to see French-Canadians uniting around a standard or an ideal, a mentality or one policy, then he would rather see his compatriots divided than united. Has he forgotten, he who cannot deliver a speech without recalling the memory of Cartier and Macdonald, has he forgotten the promise of Sir Georges-Etienne Cartier, one of the fathers of confederation? When Sir Georges-Etienne Cartier was approached for limiting the number of members to 65 in the province of Quebec, is it not true, he replied, that we could secure the triumph of the just claims of French-Canadians in the province of Quebec by the formation of a solid "bloc"? He did not want to say it would be a solid Liberal or Conservative "bloc," he simply said: "When your interests are threatened, you, French-Canadians, you will have no need to fear the English majority of the country, all you need do is to form a solid "bloc" around your national flag and your ideal and there is no party that can win or hold its place at Ottawa if it lacks the support of the province of Quebec." Is it not true that the future justified him? Is it not true that the Conservative party only succeeded in achieving power temporarily in 1911 and in 1930, thanks to the province of Quebec? Without the province of Quebec, were it not for the mistake made by that province in 1911 when it voted against reciprocity-which the prime minister hopes for now-were it not for the mistake made by the province of Quebec in 1911 which made us lose twenty years' benefits which would have accrued from that reciprocity treaty, were it not for the mistake made by the province of Quebec in 1930, the Conservative party would never have been solidly maintained in power. My hon. friend from Quebec West is wrong in fearing the union of his French-Canadian compatriots. It seems to me it is not important and necessary to the extent of wanting to immolate and sacrifice the French-Canadian minority in the country in order to achieve one's political ends.

Hear, hear.

Redistribution-Mr. Ferland

There are
others also who are afraid. Unfortunately, they are not all in their seats.

They have
the shivers.

One of
your friends, Mr. Chairman, made a rather witty remark in your presence, a remark that characterizes-
Since my hon. friend has concluded his remarks about me, would he allow me to ask him a question?
Certainly.

He complains
of the manner his county was arranged: Is he aware that this readjustment is absolutely in line with the suggestion which the former Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) made in this house on May 23, 1933?

The hon.
minister will force me to say something.

I know
that speech. After all, one must choose the lesser of two evils. I would rather have Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm than to see L'Assomption sacrificed and the people of that county smothered in the population of Montreal or compelled to go to the Laurentians, to St. Jerome or Terrebonne.
I believe, sir, one of your friends made a rather witty remark in your presence that characterizes the situation respecting all the poisonous matter contained in this bill. I do not assert it was in your presence. I know there were several Conservative members at the committee. He said jokingly and laughingly: Look at the map of Richmond-Wolfe and tell me whether the arrow (Lafleche) does not point to the scene of the crime. My hon. friend from Richmond-Wolfe is one of our most sympathetic colleagues in the House of Commons. I have had occasion to travel quite often with him for several years. I esteem him very much, but it seems to me that he also, although he is a physician and capable of curing himself, it seems to me he is afraid of swallowing the pill at the next election; he has taken care to reduce the size of his county and he is also afraid of returning before the same electors.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken forty minutes. He may continue after one of his colleagues has spoken.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on behalf of the county of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot which is
described in appendix No. 39 of the bill. First, I would like to make a few observations respecting the designation of this county. As one may read in the bill, the new county consists of:
1.	Of the largest part of the present county of St. Hyacinthe, from the standpoint of population;
2.	Of the entire county of Bagot;
3.	Of a comparatively large section of the county of Rouville.
I think it would be but fair that the designation of this new county should take in the name of Rouville into account and I can see no objection to that as in certain other counties the names of three counties are retained. In the case of the hon. member who spoke before me, his county bears the name of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. In other cases, four names are retained. One must remember that part of the county of Rouville remaining attached to St. Hyacinthe, as defined in the bill just presented, is fairly large. As a matter of fact, this part of the county of Rouville comprises more than one-third and almost one-half of the total population of this county, that is to say about 5,000 souls or, more exactly, 4,938.
It seems useless at this late hour to cover once more the whole ground of discussion that has taken place on this score, but if as claimed, it was absolutely necessary that Bagot should be annexed to St. Hyacinthe, to which I personally have no objections, I conceive it might have been difficult to retain Bagot intact, St. Hyacinthe intact and Rouville intact. But when- this bill involving the remaking of the electoral map was first considered, when there was talk of annexing part of the county of Bagot to St. Hyacinthe, I took, in company with my colleague from Bagot, steps and made representations, both orally and in writing, to the committee charged with the task of readjusting the representation in the province of Quebec, to the effect that if Bagot must of necessity form part of the county of St. Hyacinthe, they should respect the entity of the two counties, that is to say, maintain Bagot in its entirety and St. Hyacinthe in its entirety.
They granted my request with respect to Bagot and also in regard to one parish in St. Hyacinthe, that of St. Damase, which they wanted to annex to St. Johns, but they did not grant my request respecting the remainder of the county of St. Hyacinthe or the county of Rouville. As I stated previously, I regret it, as the county of St. Hyacinthe, like that of Rouville, is one of the oldest in the province
Redistribution-Mr. Dubois

of Quebec, and never had been subdivided before. It is partitioned in this bill, and this should never have been done, neither in the case of St. Hyacinthe nor that of Rouville.
I will not further discuss St. Hyacinthe, as everything that had to be said was said and repeated, but I subscribe fully to the remarks, observations and protests made in that connection by the hon. members for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) and for Bagot (Mr. Dumaine). I have myself registered my protests in that respect, both orally and in writing. But the point I do wish to stress at this stage is the fact that while they leave me part of Rouville which I accept with pleasure, they take from me an important section of the county of St. Hyacinthe which they should have left in this new county. And I do not think my colleague whom I esteem very much, the hon. Minister of Marine, could have objected to that. He keeps as his share in the county of Rouville a larger section than the section which he leaves in St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. Matters should have been left as they were, and as I told the members of the committee when I voiced my protest, if changes were necessary, they should have respected the entity and present limits of Rouville, St. Hyacinthe and Bagot. That part of Rouville *which is left to me is very important, not only from the standpoint of population but also by reason of the fact it contains three prosperous parishes and two or three large villages, one of which is the seat of the principal business college in the county of Rouville, a college well known throughout the province and even in the United States.
If one -takes the population figure of that region into account, it would be proper to retain in the designation of the new county of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot the memory of the county of Rouville. I think it would be quite possible to say: St. Hyacinthe-Bagot-Rouville, is we will say:- Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-jalm. I reiterate I can see no objection why the designation of the county could not be altered in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Does
she hon. member believe we could use the word Rouville in the designation of two counties in the same province? There is already Chamibly-Rouville. That part of Rouville annexed to Chambly comprises a population of 8,838 citizens. Is it not more fitting to use the word Rouville with Chambly and to leave the words St. Hyacinthe-Bagot? It must not be forgotten that the word Rouville is already on the map with Chambly-Rouville.

Mr. Chairman, I fully understand the hon. minister's reply when he remarks that the part of Rouville remaining in the county of Chambly is larger than the section joined with the county of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I also understand that if it were a case of annexing only a couple of parishes it would perhaps not be necessary to add the name, but I think one must consider that the part of Rouville remaining with St. Hyacinthe-Bagot constitutes more than one third and almost half its population,-almost 5,000. That part is not quite as large as the part of Rouville joined with the hon. minister's county, but I believe the hon. minister should not object to the word " Rouville " oeing used twice in the province. If there was any confusion, one could possibly add the words Rouville East, Which does not appear necessary to me. There should be no objection to this word being repeated in two counties, following the practice that prevails in certain parts of large cities, such as Winnipeg and others; and that is what I request.

Before recording a final protest against the bill under discussion, you will allow me to make a rectification. At page 5695 of unrevised Hansard, French edition, I stated in reply to a question of the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duran-leau) that the total population of Nicolet, following redistribution, would be 47,000 and a few odd hundreds. As I gave those figures from memory, I confounded the 1921 census returns with those for 1931. The total population of Nicolet-Yamaska after the coming redistribution, with the union of Nicolet and Yamaska, will be exactly 43,493, which is about the normal unit for the province.
I repeat I do not understand why six parishes are taken from the county of Nicolet and a half parish from the county of Yamaska, when these two counties united completely would only form a population of 45,493.

Will the hon. member allow me? The hon. Solicitor-General (Mr. Dupre) moves that the Committee report progress and the Speaker take the chair for a few minutes. The hon. member may then continue his remarks.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I desire to thank the hon. gentleman who was speaking for his courtesy in this matter.	-

Mr. Chairman, in the course of my sipeech last Tuesday,
I believe I treated my hon. friends with all possible politeness, kindness and courtesy. I stated my case most earnestly when I asked the hon. gentlemen to reconsider their decision with respect to the county of Nicolet-Yamiaska. I see by the newly printed amendments that no change has been made in Nico-let or Yamaska. Will the hon. Minister of Marine tell me why, having regard to the normal population of Nicolet-Yamaska, the committee decided to take away half the small parish of St. Michel? Can the hon. minister tell me why that was done?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The
hon. member knows perfectly that I was not a member of the committee, and in order to answer him, we would have to discuss once more the map of that whole region of the province of Quebec. However, I will tell my hon. friend: Had we not detached a few parishes from the county of Nicolet and annexed them to Lotbiniere, the hon. member would have noted that Lotbiniere had a much smaller population than that of Nicolet-Yamaska. Even with the addition of several
parishes from Nicolet to the county of Lotbiniere, this county has a population of only 38,546. As I stated m the course of this debate, we wanted to give the citizens of the province a unit of representation that was as equitable as possible. That is the reason why a few parishes of Nicolet were united with Lotbiniere.
Why half a parish?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not know that detail.

Mr. Chairman,
I cannot accept this reply from the hon. Minister of Marine. If he really wanted to do justice to me and the people of my county, he could have used his influence with the members of the committee on redistribution. When he tells me he acted thus merely to equalize the population of the county of Lotbiniere with the population of the adjoining counties, I think the hon. minister gives a rather specious answer. The county of Lotbiniere, minus the population of 5,000 taken from the county of Nicolet, would still have a population of 33,000, which is larger than the population of Dorchester, Argenteuil and other counties. The county of Nicolet by retaining its entire present population and the present population of the county of Yamaska, will still have a population of only 45,493, which is a smaller population than that of the counties of Charlcvoix-Saguenay, Drummond-Arthabaska, Chicoutimi, and that of many other counties. I believe I can detect the whole manoeuvre underlying this matter. Half of the parish of St. Michel is taken from the county of Yamaska, because it is a Liberal parish. Six parishes, also Liberal, are taken from my county. And why? Unless it be to create a fief, a safe constituency for the future Conservative candidate. And when the hon Minister of Marine dares accuse us, Liberals, of only playing politics in connection with this bill, I ask myself what one must call this method of dealing with the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska.

It is an
abomination!

It is a
national crime!

I protest once more and as strongly as I can against the present bill No. 2. The people of my county and those of the county of Yamaska are being treated unjustly. In support of my renewed protest, I will read to this house a last appeal
Redistribution-Mr. Dubois

of the people of the county of Nicolet. Here is the telegram which I received in that connection :
Mr. L. Dubois,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
We are sending you copy of a message forwarded to the right hon. prime minister and we urgently request you to use all your influence to secure justice for us. Here is the text of the message addressed to the prime minister. Mr. Premier, respectful representations have been made to your Government asking that the county of Nicolet which has a sufficient population be retained as a distinct entity, but if a union is necessary the two counties of Nicolet and Yamaska should be united in their entirety. We had understood your Government had condescended to adopt the second alternative that was so just and legitimate in every respect and decided to merge completely the two counties of Nicolet and Yamaska. To our surprise, the bill as presented dismembers and subdivides not only the counties of Nicolet and Yamaska but also the diocese of Nicolet by the annexation of half a parish to the county of Richelieu. St-Hyacinthe diocese, and of six parishes to the county of Lotbiniere, diocese of Quebec. We believe it sufficient to point out this involuntary error in order for you to have it corrected in such a manner as to give complete satisfaction to the interested authorities and taxpayers. We are submitting the same request to your French-speaking colleagues and to the member for Nicolet. We remain,
H. N. Biton, mayor,
J. Alfred Gaudet, barrister, Secretary-Treasurer of the Municipality of the Town of Nicolet.
I will point out that this Mr J. Alfred Gaudet, barrister, is the very man who was my opponent in 1930 and I must bear witness in this house to the fact that he is no coward.
I must bear witness that he had enough courage and honesty not to ask for the dismemberment of the county of Nicolet. Mr. Gaudet is ready to run again at the next election, with the same county and same parishes which he faced in 1930.

He is
courageous.

I am convinced this dismemberment effected in the county of Nicolet and in the county of Yamaska was requested by Mr. Comtois, defeated candidate in the county of Yamaska. This gentleman has not the courage to again face all his electors of 1930, and to-day he asks the Government to dismember the county of Yamaska and the county of Nicolet, in order to try and secure a somewhat safer riding for himself. I have no compliments to pay to the gentleman, but I am proud to be able to say that my opponent of 1930 appears to me to be much more courageous than the candidate who was defeated in the county of Yamaska.

Those petitions which I mentioned the other day, those resolutions and telegrams were sent to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and to the members of the committee, and I observe that those documents received no consideration whatever. They were thrown into the waste paper basket and no recommendation was taken into account. They preferred deciding with a ruling majority to drive six parishes out of the county of Nicolet and expel half the parish of St. Michel from the county of Yamaska. I understand, sir, that those sitting on your right are mighty enough to do such things, but magnanimous people can never be made to understand that might is right. I ask that Bill No. 2 be modified. The clause that reads as follows:
This Act may be cited as The Representation Act. 1933, should read: The Deportation Act, 1933.
Hear, hear.

I consider it
most deplorable that six parishes in the lower part of my county and the parish of St. Michel should be compelled to form part of other counties at the next election when they expressed the explicit desire to remain with their old counties. This bill is a cowardly, deceitful and felonious measure. In order to justify the expulsion of these parishes they try to make me and my people believe that this is being done to establish a uniform unit of representation in the province of Quebec. What deceit! I am about through, Mr. Chairman, and if you will allow me, I will make a comparison. On September 5, 1755, more than 400 Acadians were assembled in the little church at Grand-Pre. Winslow who was instructed to read Lawrence's orders to the little gathering deprived of all means of resistance was seated at a table in the aisle. One of my ancestors formed part of the group. That night, the clock struck the end of century of tranquillity and happiness. The following morning, those poor Acadians were looking at their homes and farms for the last time. They were being expelled. And it happened to be a Saturday, just like today! I need not tell you that history branded the perpetrators of that villainy of 1755.

Mr. Chairman, before this appendix of the redistribution bill relating to the province of Quebec is adopted, I trust you will allow me to add a word of protest against this government's arbitrary measure that involves the disappearance of the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm as an entity.

Redistribution-Mr. Fafard
The first project conceived by the Conservative party which had sworn to wipe out the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm, involved originally the union of Montcalm .with the county of Joliette and the annexation of L'Assomption with Maisonneuve.
The attention of these gentlemen having been called to the absurdity of uniting an essentially rural county with a city county, they deemed fit to give up this ridiculous project and to add the county of L'Assomption to that of Terrebonne.
It is true, concessions were made when they agreed to give up this more or less stupid second alternative and not separate the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm whose common interests require that its component parts remain united, but take the whole county of L'Assomption-Montcalm and join it with the county of Joliette.
Viewed from certain angles this project might appear rational and, of the three proposals I believe it should be in the interests of the people of the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm.
Yet, I do not want to be understood as exonerating the heads of the administration who apply the saying: "Might is right," and unite two electoral districts whose respective populations are sufficient to secure each one its separate existence, particularly when one considers the Conservatives create under the present bill a new electoral district, that of Chapleau, whose population is smaller than that of the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm by 9,000, and smaller than that of Joliette by 71)00. and when this same bill provides for the maintenance of the county of Argenteuil as a separate entity with a population of less than 20,000.
The present government realizing* its unpopularity by reason of the complete failure to implement any of its promises, is trying by all possible means and every possible injustice to mend its fences. Allow, me to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that the Conservative party has so deceived the people, that no matter what it may do, the next appeal to them will witness its defeat, and with all due deference to my hon. friend, the Solicitor-General, despite the efforts he and the honourable French-Canadian ministers have made to improve their prospects, it might well happen that the province of Quebec may once more form a solid bloc to show it cannot be deceived with impunity. Moreover, when the province of Quebec forms a solid bloc it has good reasons for doing so.
If I am bound, sir, to accept the provisions of the present bill that are imposed on us,
I must inform you again that it is simply a case of choosing the lesser of two evils. My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. Ferland) and myself cannot help but feel the insult that each of our electoral districts suffers in not being allowed to retain their respective identities although they both had an absolute right to remain as they were.
Those are, Mr. Chairman, the few remarks I wished to make before the adoption of the appendix to the bill respecting the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, I would be lacking in dignity were I to complain about the treatment I have been subjected to. I do not intend complaining about what was done to me as member for L'lslet. Therefore I wish to protest once more on behalf of the county of L'lslet against the political crime that is about to be perpetrated.
Since it is the last time the county of L'lslet, as a county, may be heard in the House of Commons of Canada, I want the last words I am to speak to be devoid of bitterness. I simply want to avail myself of this opportunity to thank the people of L'lslet for the confidence they have reposed in me since 1917. I thank the Liberals, I thank the Conservatives; they were both excellent soldiers and on the morrow of the battle, they knew how to join hands and work for the prosperity of their district. I also wish to thank my colleagues for the support they have given me. I thank particularly the hon. members for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who lent me their full support in trying to preserve the beautiful and historic county of L'lslet. Unfortunately, we failed to achieve the results we were seeking, but I am proud of one thing, we did not get on our knees, we remained standing.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to
avail myself of the precedent established last night by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short). I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bagot (Mr. Dumaine), that number forty of the schedule for Quebec be amended by adding the word " Napierville " after the words " St. Johns-Iberville." This would give the new constituency the following denomination, "St. Johns-Iberville-Napierville."
Amendment (Mr. Dupuis) agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, there have been some petitions tabled which were in proper form. They were signed by interested
Redistribution Bill

parties, people living in the four parishes which are to be taken away from the constituency of Temiscouata. They were signed by both Conservatives and Liberals. The clerk of the house said that they were presented in regular form. I will therefore ask of the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) three questions: first, what has been done with those petitions? Second, why have they been disregarded? Third, at whose request?
I have nothing to answer. I do not know what has been done with those petitions.
Who knows about them?
I am not supposed to take care of them. They are not under my care.

That is the answer Cain gave about Abel:	"Am I my brother's
keeper?"
I rise to a point of order. Surely, to compare a minister of the crown with Cain is unparliamentary.
Is the hon. gentleman the guardian of the Solicitor General?
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, kindly to see that those words are withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the comparison in the way it was used by the hon. member for Temiscouata was unparliamentary.
Toutes les comparaisons ne sont pas odieuses.
I will ask another question of the Solicitor General. The government aas enfranchised the Indians-
I will tell my hon. friend at once that this is not a court and I shall not stand for any cross-examination from him.

I have never in my life
seen anyone so dumb.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I have just a few remarks .to offer. It was suggested this morning by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) that the addition of L'Assomption-Montcalm to Joliette had been done practically at my suggestion. That is not representing exactly what I had said. If the report of my observations is read carefully it will be very clearly understood that my suggestion, made with a view to reaohing a compromise, was this: First of all I object to the disappearance of the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm. I contended that it should be kept as it was because of its importance for comparison with other constituencies. But I said that if the county of L'Assomption-Montoalm had to disappear it should disappear by being joined in its entirety with the county of Joliette. I said that this would create a large county, but it would not be the only county with a large population. My suggestion was made in order not to destroy the limits of the constituencies as they exist at the present time. I object to a part of the county only being taken to be added to an adjoining constituency. That was my main contention. My suggestion was that L'Assomption-Montcalm should be added to the county of Joliette in its entirety rather than be divided up, and that all the other constituencies in the northern section of the province be kept in their entirety without any subtractions from their territory. But in the reprinted bill which we have before us I find that that part of my suggestion has not been carried out. It is true that the county of Labelle is going to remain in the same condition as it is at the present time, and the same is true of the county of Argenteuil and of the county of Terrebonne, but that is not the case with Laval-Two Mountains. That county is being changed. Two parishes from the north of the county, the municipality of St. Colom-ban and the municipality of St. Canut are being added to the county of Argenteuil. It is a matter of only one thousand of a population; it does not amount to very
Redistribution Bill

much; so why change it, and two other parishes in Laval-Two Mountains are being transferred over the river Desprairies to Mercier on the island of Montreal. We have all been complaining that the population in the island of Montreal was large enough, and *it was due to that fact that we had difficulty in adjusting the rural seats in the province of Quebec. If that is the case, and we are all agreed on that, those two municipalities transferred should have been left in the county of Two Mountains.
What is going to be the result of this? We are increasing the population of many constituencies in the province of Quebec, because we say they are not large enough as compared with others, but, in the case of Laval-Two Mountains, the population is being reduced. We are making a large county of L'Assomption-Montcalm-Joliette, giving that new county a population of over fifty thousand, and we are destroying the limits of the county of Laval-Two Mountains and reducing its population to 25,000. The population of Laval-Two Mountains in the reprinted bill which is going to pass, because nobody can prevent it passing now, if the government is determined to put it through, is reduced by nearly five thousand. The population of the constituency of my hon. friend the Postmaster General is going to have a population of
25.000,	and the adjoining county of Terrebone
35.000,	and the new Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is going to have over 50,000. That is the kind of a redistribution which is presently offered. Hon. gentlemen opposite always speak of equalizing populations. That was to be their main objective so far as possible. But everybody can see in what way they are equalizing the population in the different constituencies in the province of Quebec. They are equalizing the population where equalizing is to their advantage, and reducing the population when they think they can derive from it a certain political advantage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With the consent of the right hon. gentleman I should like to make a brief statement which may shorten this discussion. With respect to the constituency of Prince Albert, to which my right hon. friend has referred, so far as possible having regard to the redistribution as arranged we have endeavoured to meet the views of the right hon. gentleman. A few days ago it was suggested that the southern boundary of Prince Albert had been fixed in 1914, when both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and myself were members of the committee under the government of Sir Robert Borden. I suppose it is unnecessary to remind the right hon. gentleman or this committee that since 1911 two censuses have been taken, one in 1921 and the other in 1931, and obviously during that period of twenty years, with the increase in population which has taken place the boundaries of most of the constituencies must be altered if regard is had to the unit of population. In 1914 the southern boundary of Prince Albert, as perhaps the right hon.
Redistribution Bill

gentleman will observe, commenced at the extreme eastern' boundary of the province and then moved straight west, forming the southern boundary of several constituencies as well as the boundary of Prince Albert. The 1924 redistribution did not affect the southern boundary of the constituencies of Melfort and Prince Albert as they had been constituted. Unfortunately, with regard to our being able to meet the wishes of the right hon. gentleman, I only desire to point out that the shifting of the population in the last ten years has involved the adjustment of boundaries and the increase of representation. On the new map-and I went into it with some degree of care-there is built up a new constituency called Rosthern which, if one has regard to the returns in former elections, will return a Liberal candidate with a substantial majority. Unless there is a change in the voting sentiments of that population there is very little doubt, according to past returns, that a Liberal candidate will be returned in this constituency. The town of Rosthern lies within the present constituency of Prince Albert, under the redistribution of 1914, and is north of the line fixed in that year. The redistribution measure now before the house involves moving the line, which is the southern boundary of Prince Albert, twenty-four miles north, which would leave the town of Rosthern in the new constituency of the same name.
If the right hon. gentleman will pardon me, the southern boundary is moved only twelve miles north.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Pardon me; I should
have said twelve miles, and I thank the hon. gentleman. I now suggest, in order at least partially to meet the views of the right hon. gentleman and his friends, that the southern boundary of Prince Albert be moved north not twelve miles but six miles only.
That is correct; it was twenty-four miles previously and now it is twelve miles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is what I thought; my memory is fairly good. I was right in that we moved the southern boundary line of Prince Albert twenty-four miles north in the original draft; that is, four townships of six miles each. I now suggest that instead of moving the boundary line twenty-four miles north we meet the right hon. gentleman half way and move it only twelve miles north. Instead of carrying it straight through to the point of intersection with the boundary of Melfort, it is now proposed that we proceed east as far as the Duck Lake reserve, then

up the side of that reserve and easterly until we strike the river, and then proceed downstream to the point of intersection with the westerly boundary of Melfort. The effect of that will be to throw out a triangular piece of territory in which I am told, according to the last election returns, there was a majority adverse to the right hon. gentleman of about 250. Instead of the line being moved twenty-four miles north, therefore, it would be moved only twelve miles north, and the town of Rosthern would be included in the new constituency of the same name, which has been built up. Instead of proceeding east in a straight line to the intersection of the constituency of Melfort, when the boundary reached the Duck Lake reserve it would proceed downstream to the western boundary of the riding of Melfort. I believe this will not make any appreciable difference to the right hon. gentleman from the standpoint of voting power; the population in that triangular strip of land to which I have referred, lying south and east of the Duck Lake reserve, between that reserve and the point of intersection with the Saskatchewan river, will be withdrawn from that constituency.
I may tell the committee frankly that it is quite impossible to readjust the boundaries without involving a general change, and those who have followed the matter know that this results very largely from what was done with regard to the constituency of Melville. Because of what was done in that regard the plans have been entirely changed, because it must be remembered that this is a redistribution not of seats but rather of population. That is the difficulty in Saskatchewan. There is no change in the number of seats but there is a change with regard to population. The whole difficulty arises because of the need to equalize as nearly as possible the population in the various ridings. With regard to Melville we have yielded to popular clamour; hon. members from Saskatchewan have been most insistent that Melville should remain unchanged. They have importuned members of the government; they have told us that if this were done all would be well. Man after man spoke to me and asked me if I did not think this should be done. I foresaw what would happen; the result has been exactly what I expected. Those who listened to the address delivered in this house the night before last by one w'ho was thus accommodated will realize how sound was the view I took. I only mention this in passing, and I want to say that I have done the very best I could, conscientiously and carefully. I consulted my friends on the committee, not only the hon.

Redistribution Bill
gentleman Who sits to my right at the moment (Mr. Turnbull) but others as well, and. so far as I can see the only way to meet the situation is by moving the line only half the twenty-four miles originally suggested. This will compensate for not bringing it the whole distance that the right hon. gentleman is suggesting. We are giving half the territory that lies to the south and east of the Duck Lake reserve and between there and the western boundary of Melfort and south of the river. As I say, I have done this after consultation with the members of the committee and with a most earnest desire to meet the wishes of the right hon. gentleman so far as I could having regard to the fact that the constituency of Rosthern had been built in. The last election returns indicate that this territory would be favourable to the opposition. As was originally intended, the town of Rosthern would be within this territory. I have done the best that could be done under the circumstances and have endeavoured to make an equitable disposition by making certain changes in the original electoral map.

Mr. Chairman, for the time and trouble which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and those associated with him have given to the matter of the readjustment of the boundaries of Prince Albert constituency, I should like to thank them. I appreciate what has been done, although it is far from meeting the views which I expressed as to what I thought would be fair and just. Nevertheless, it is a change for the better as compared with the boundaries of the constituency as contained in the original report of the special committee to this house, and which the Prime Minister himself quite frankly stated were recognized as not satisfactory boundaries even from the point of view of the government. They were not boundaries that were intended to be retained, and they were evidently put there at the beginning for the purpose of negotiation and were kept there when in some particulars the negotiations broke down. May I say to the Prime Minister that while he says that he has met me half way, as far as half of the southern portion of the constituency is concerned, he may have met me in part half way geographically, but he has been very far from meeting me half way politically. After all, the political is the important consideration in studying the effects of any redistribution.
It will I think be recalled that my suggestion was that first of all there should be no additional territory added to the constituency of Prince Albert. The other point which I pressed most strongly was that the southern
boundary of Prince Albert constituency as it is at present should be retained. The part lying immediately to the north of the southern boundary of the present constituency has been taken away in part for twelve miles to the north, in part for more than double that distance. This is the strong Liberal portion of the constituency, and it will affect the Liberal candidate, whoever he may be, most seriously. The government is adding to the eastern side of the constituency of Prince Albert certain territory from Melfort. It is true that under the revision the extent of this added territory will not be as large as was previously intended. It is also true that what is now being added will add a small Liberal majority. Based on the figures of 1930, it would be something like 50. This is being done instead of adding a Conservative majority of twice or three times as much as would have been the case under the bill as introduced. A portion of the additional territory which it was proposed to add and which gave a Conservative majority remains under the revise in the constituency of Melfort. As I have said, a portion giving a Liberal majority of 50 comes into Prince Albert. The effect with respect to what is being done in the southern portion of the constituency is however quite serious, in what it wipes out of the Liberal majority in the constituency itself. The figures for the 1930 election will bear me out. The Liberal majority in Prince Albert in the 1930 election was 1,192 whereas the redistribution as it is now made would give with the added 50 Liberal majority in what is being added from Melfort a Conservative majority of 136.

I suggest that if my
right hon. friend would check those figures again he will find that they are not exactly correct. According to the figures I have, it is the other way around.
